Breaking: Australian Army soldier dies, five injured in NT training incident
An Australian Army soldier has died in a training incident at the Mount Bundey Training Area in the Northern Territory.
In a statement, Defence says five other army soldiers were were injured in the incident which happened yesterday.
The department says next of kin has been notified and the family has request privacy.
"Defence can confirm an Australian Army soldier has died during a training exercise at the Mount Bundey Training Area on 5 October 2026," the statement said.

"Five other Australian Army soldiers were injured. Next of kin has been notified."We request that the privacy of Defence members and families is respected at this time. Defence will provide further updates when possible."

Analysis: OpenAI hoped for a warm welcome. Instead it's going to face a tough crowd
It is a bruised OpenAI that is set to limp into the Australian political spotlight today.
It had been pencilled in for a centre stage performance, tapping into a bit of Silicon Valley star power, to convince Australians they should want the AI company to make our nation its second home.
But it is hard to imagine a worse warm up act than Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's announcement that OpenAI's agents had "hacked" into a Medicare statistics website making global headlines.
It wasn't exactly a digital armageddon, given the incident was neither particularly sophisticated nor revealed anything of importance. Even though it was quite novel and a taste of things to come.
But you wouldn't have known from the whack Albanese gave the company amid his global push for AI regulation.

Shadow cabinet meeting to finalise migration policy
The ABC understands the shadow ministry is currently meeting to finalise the Coalition's migration policy set to be released today.
The opposition is expected to announce it intends to cut net overseas migration to 100,000 in its first year in government if elected.
Nine newspapers report the migration intake will then be tied to housing completions, which they've previously announced.
Hanson accuses Coalition of copying One Nation's migration policy
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has accused the Coalition of turning up late to the debate on migration and copying her party's policy.
The Coalition will announce its migration policy today.
We expect it'll announce a plan to cut net overseas migration to 100,000 in its first year of government if elected.

"The Coalition has turned up late to the grand final after both teams have headed back to the changerooms, waving a photocopy of One Nation's immigration policy," Hanson said."Their plan is to build more houses, then bring in more people to compete for them."

"Their plan is to build more houses, then bring in more people to compete for them."
Wilson says migration policy to focus on advancing national interest
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has appeared on News24, where he's detailed the aims of the Coalition's migration policy.
The Coalition is expected to announce it intends to cut net overseas migration to 100,000 in its first year in government if elected.
Nine newspapers report that number will then be tied to the Coalition's plan to cap migration to housing completions.
It comes weeks after One Nation and Labor announced plans to curb migration.
Wilson has told News24 the policy will focus on advancing social, economic and cultural integration and the economy.
"The sole purpose of a migration program is to advance Australia's national interest," Wilson says.

"In doing so we have to make sure we get the labour that farmers need, we need to make sure we get the skills to build more houses that Australians need and particularly to make sure there's a relationship between our migrations numbers and our housing stock."
Sharma says he expects economic modelling to form part of migration announcement
Shadow Assistant Minister Dave Sharma says the Coalition party room will be meeting to discuss its migration policy set to be announced today.
The ABC understands the Coalition is expected to announce it intends to cut net overseas migration to 100,000 in the first year if it was to win the election.
The shadow home affairs minister has this morning flagged the Coalition will target visa-overstayers as part of its policy.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Sharma says he doesn't think One Nation has driven its migration policy.
Sharma says he expects the Coalition's economic modelling to form part of the announcement today.
"The challenge for us as the Coalition is to convince people why we would be a better alternative government to that that's currently in office," Sharma says.
"That's the challenge for any opposition and I think showing the public that we are prepared to put Australia's national interests first."
Keogh says government is looking to regulate veteran advocate sector
Veterans' Affairs Minister Matt Keogh says the government is looking at ways to regulate to the veterans' advocate sector.

A Four Corners investigation has found that for-profit companies are targeting veterans with offers of free Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA) funded services while allegedly delivering bare minimum care.
The investigation found the companies have offered gifts and raffle tickets to win over their care plans.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Keogh says he's concerned the allegation will create a feel of distrust in the veteran community about the services offered.
He says the government has engaged the Australian Federal Police in some cases to crack down on providers.

"We've also got to make sure that we're working to make sure that those medical providers that are doing the wrong thing and companies that are working with them trying to take advantage of veterans are not able to do that," Keogh says.
"And we're doing that through a range of ways. Some of that is directly engaging with those providers. Some of it is also working through the Fraud Fusion Task Force."

Duniam flags visa-overstayers to be target of Coalition migration policy
Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam has confirmed the Coalition will release its long-awaited migration policy today.
The ABC understands the Coalition is expected to announce it intends to cut migration to 100,000 in the first year after an election.
Speaking to News24, the shadow minister says he won't release the numbers until he steps up to speak sometime today.
Duniam has hinted the Coalition will seek to target visa-overstayers who have exhausted their appeal rights.
He says the Coalition has been engaging with the Parliamentary Budget Office and has pledged the full costings closer to the election.

"I think Australians expect the immigration system to be robust, to have integrity and of course that means when someone reaches the end of their legitimate time here in Australia, whether that be as a visitor, a student, some other form of temporary visa, they go home," Duniam says.
Joyce says reported Coalition migration policy shows 'endorsement' of One Nation
The Coalition hasn't released its migration policy just yet but One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has been out this morning to have his take on it.
The opposition will release its long-awaited migration policy today, weeks after One Nation and Labor released theirs.
At least two newspapers are reporting the Coalition will seek to cut migration to 100,000 in the first year following an election.
That number would then increase based on the number of annual housing completions, according to the reports.
Speaking to Channel Nine, Joyce says the policy appears to be similar to One Nation's plan.
"It's a bit like the grand finals over and then the third team's turned up and everybody's left the stage and no one's clapping," Joyce says.
"I congratulate the Coalition for basically coming up with our policy. There's a bit of a nuance in there, but you know what? It shows an endorsement of where One Nation is off to."
AI executives to appear before parliamentary inquiry
Executives from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google will today appear at a parliamentary inquiry examining the risks and upsides of artificial intelligence.

Labor MP Jo Briskey, who chairs the joint select committee into AI, says it will give parliamentarians an opportunity to question OpenAI executives about a hack on a Services Australia portal in June.
The federal government became aware of the breach when the artificial intelligence company informed Australian in September.
OpenAI made a public apology to the Australian government for the hack.
Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Briskey says the committee will be interested to know what steps the company has taken to prevent a similar hack from reoccurring.
"I think it's important that everyone appearing before the inquiry across our public hearings come prepared to answer questions that committee members have of them," Briskey says.
Albanese, leaders head to Tuvalu for Pacific pre-COP event
One of the world's least-visited countries will receive global attention today as it hosts Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and 13 other world leaders for high-level climate talks.
The trip is part of this week's pre-COP meeting, which is aimed at showing the world how warmer temperatures are threatening the existence of small island communities.
The turnout of global leaders has been slightly smaller than expected, with the prime minister of Mauritius and president of Timor Leste the only non-Pacific heads of state attending.
Tuvalu is on the front line of climate change, with rising seas, coastal erosion and extreme weather already forcing people to leave the nation.
The Albanese government has been criticised for only attracting a handful of prime ministers and presidents despite spending $20 million on the event.
Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said it was the wish of Pacific leaders to broaden the invitation list, and that world leaders typically don't get invited to pre-COP events.
Wallace says migration policy will be revealed today
Liberal MP Andrew Wallace says the Coalition's migration policy will be targeted to ensure the right number of people enter the country.
The Coalition will announce its long-awaited migration policy today, weeks after Labor and One Nation announced their policy.
Two newspapers are reporting the Coalition will seek to cut the migration number to 100,000 in its first year of government before capping it to housing completions.
Asked on Channel Nine if the policy has been modelled for the impact to the Australian economy, Wallace says that will be revealed today.

"You can't just slash immigration altogether. We've got to ensure that our farmers and our key industries have the right skills to be able to keep the country moving, and that's what we'll be focused on," Wallace says.
